title: 🔬 Workflows & Demonstrations
text:
🖥️ The User Interface
ADMETShiny (Version 1.0.0) is an open-source R Shiny web application designed for the management, calculation, filtering, and selection of drug-like molecules in early-stage drug discovery.






Navigation bar
The top horizontal bar is divided into seven numbered modules, each marked with a green hex icon:








#
Module
Purpose




1
Home
Returns to the main landing page


2
ADMET Master Manager
Calculates and analyzes molecular properties


3
CDK & webchem
Cheminformatics tools for structure processing and chemical analysis


4
Report
Customizes and exports analysis results


5
About
Project and author information


6
First Steps
Step-by-step tutorials for new users


7
Documentation
Technical guides and vignettes





Landing page panels
Below the navigation bar, the dashboard is split into two sections:









Note📝 Description



Summarizes the app’s integration of bioinformatics and cheminformatics workflows for molecular descriptor visualization.










Tip📖 How to cite?



Provides the formal 2026 academic citation and the GitHub repository link.

title: 🔬 Workflows & Demonstrations
text:
🧪 The Dataset Example
The Drug-likeness Filters section lets users apply customizable filters based on popular medicinal chemistry criteria:

✅ Lipinski
✅ Veber
✅ Ghose
✅ Egan
✅ Muegge

Adjustable thresholds are available for maximum molecular weight, logP, hydrogen bond acceptors/donors, and maximum Lipinski violations.






Filtered results
The central area displays the Filtered Results table under the Filtered Molecules tab (6), giving a structured overview of the compounds that meet the selected criteria. This interactive data grid shows key molecular descriptors:

Molecule ID
Canonical SMILES
Chemical formula
Molecular weight (MW)
Number of heavy atoms
Number of aromatic heavy atoms







Tip🔍 Quick search



Use the Search bar (8) at the top right of the table to filter molecules by name, SMILES string, or specific properties.


The top tabs, Data Preview (5) and Plots (7), let you toggle seamlessly between the raw dataset, refined subsets, and data distributions, providing an intuitive, integrated workflow for compound prioritization.

title: Learning Guide
text: This document provides detailed tutorials for every function in the admetshiny package.

title: Learning Guide
text:
Installation

# From CRAN (when available)
install.packages("admetshiny")

# From GitHub
# devtools::install_github("xavierclementegarcia/admetshiny")

title: Learning Guide
text:
Launching the Shiny App

library(admetshiny)
run_app()

title: Learning Guide
text:
Drug-Likeness Filters

lipinskiFilter()
Filters compounds according to the Rule of Five (Lipinski et al., 1997): MW <= 500, LogP <= 5, HBA <= 10, HBD <= 5.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 600, 450),
  LogP = c(2, 7, 4),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 12, 6),
  `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 5, 3),
  `Lipinski #violations` = c(0, 3, 0),
  check.names = FALSE)

lipinskiFilter(d)
lipinskiFilter(d, mw = 450, logp = 4)  # Custom thresholds



ghoseFilter()
Filters according to the Ghose qualifying range (1999): MW 160-480, MR 40-130, LogP -0.4 to 5.6, total atoms 20-70.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 600), MR = c(90, 150), LogP = c(2, 7),
  `#Total atoms` = c(30, 80),
  `Ghose #violations` = c(0, 4),
  check.names = FALSE)

ghoseFilter(d)



veberFilter()
Filters according to Veber (2002): RB <= 10 AND (TPSA <= 140 OR HBA+HBD <= 12).

d <- data.frame(
  TPSA = c(80, 160), `#Rotatable bonds` = c(3, 14),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 12), `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 5),
  `Veber #violations` = c(0, 1),
  check.names = FALSE)

veberFilter(d)



eganFilter()
Filters according to Egan (2000): TPSA <= 131.6, LogP <= 5.88.

d <- data.frame(
  TPSA = c(80, 160), LogP = c(2, 7),
  `Egan #violations` = c(0, 2),
  check.names = FALSE)

eganFilter(d)



mueggeFilter()
Filters according to Muegge (2001): MW 200-600, LogP -2 to 5, HBA <= 10, HBD <= 5, RB <= 15, TPSA <= 150, pharmacophore points >= 4.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 700), LogP = c(2, 7), TPSA = c(80, 160),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 12), `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 5),
  `#Rotatable bonds` = c(3, 14),
  `Muegge #violations` = c(0, 5),
  check.names = FALSE)

mueggeFilter(d)



applyFilters()
Apply multiple filters in sequence.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 600, 450), LogP = c(2, 7, 4), TPSA = c(80, 160, 100),
  MR = c(90, 150, 100),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 12, 6),
  `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 5, 3),
  `#Rotatable bonds` = c(3, 14, 5),
  `#Heavy atoms` = c(22, 80, 30),
  `Lipinski #violations` = c(0, 3, 0),
  `Ghose #violations` = c(0, 4, 0),
  `Veber #violations` = c(0, 1, 0),
  `Egan #violations` = c(0, 2, 0),
  `Muegge #violations` = c(0, 5, 0),
  check.names = FALSE)

applyFilters(d, filters = c("Lipinski", "Veber", "Egan"))



computeViolationColumns()
Computes violation columns from physicochemical properties. Preserves pre-existing violation columns.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 600), LogP = c(2, 7), TPSA = c(80, 160),
  MR = c(90, 150),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 12), `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 5),
  `#Rotatable bonds` = c(3, 14), `#Heavy atoms` = c(22, 80),
  check.names = FALSE)

d <- computeViolationColumns(d)
names(d)

title: Learning Guide
text:
Data Normalization

mapADMETColumns()
Maps any user dataset to the standard schema.

d <- data.frame(
  smiles = c("CCO", "CC(=O)O"),
  mol_weight = c(46, 60),
  logp = c(-0.3, -0.2))

mapping <- c(
  "smiles" = "SMILES",
  "mol_weight" = "MW",
  "logp" = "LogP")

d_std <- mapADMETColumns(d, mapping)



mapCDKDescriptors()
Maps CDK descriptor output to standard schema.


calcCDKDescriptors()
Calculates descriptors from SMILES using the Chemistry Development Kit.

smiles <- c("CCO", "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O")
desc <- calcCDKDescriptors(smiles, which = c("mw", "logp", "tpsa"))



getSmilesFromIdentifiers()
Retrieves SMILES from PubChem via compound names, CAS numbers, or InChIKeys.

result <- getSmilesFromIdentifiers(c("aspirin", "caffeine"))

title: Learning Guide
text:
Plots

plotBoiledEgg()
BOILED-Egg model for GI absorption and BBB permeability prediction.

# Basic usage
d <- data.frame(LogP = c(2, 5), TPSA = c(50, 150))
plotBoiledEgg(d)

# With WLOGP (uses official polygons, axis = "WLOGP")
d2 <- data.frame(
  LogP = c(1.5, 3.0, 4.5),
  WLOGP = c(1.8, 2.8, 4.2),
  TPSA = c(40, 80, 120))
plotBoiledEgg(d2)

# With P-gp substrate
d3 <- data.frame(
  LogP = c(1.5, 3.0, 4.5),
  TPSA = c(40, 80, 120),
  `Pgp substrate` = c("Yes", "No", "Yes"),
  check.names = FALSE)
plotBoiledEgg(d3)

# Suppress console statistics
plotBoiledEgg(d, console_stats = FALSE)



plotMW(), plotTPSA(), plotLogP()
Simple distribution histograms.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 320, 380, 420),
  TPSA = c(40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 50, 70, 90),
  LogP = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5))

plotMW(d)
plotTPSA(d)
plotLogP(d)



plotCorrHeatmap()
Correlation heatmap with Pearson or Spearman method and significance asterisks.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 400, 500, 350, 450),
  LogP = c(2, 3, 4, 2.5, 3.5),
  TPSA = c(60, 80, 100, 70, 90),
  MR = c(70, 90, 110, 80, 100))

# Pearson (default)
plotCorrHeatmap(d)

# Spearman
plotCorrHeatmap(d, method = "spearman")

# Custom properties
plotCorrHeatmap(d, props = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"))

# Suppress console
plotCorrHeatmap(d, console_stats = FALSE)



plotHistogramCustom()
Customizable histogram with automatic statistical test selection.

# Ungrouped: Shapiro-Wilk
d1 <- data.frame(MW = c(300, 350, 400, 320, 380, 360, 340, 370))
plotHistogramCustom(d1, variable = "MW")

# 2 groups: Wilcoxon
d2 <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 320, 350, 380, 400, 500, 520, 550, 580, 600),
  GI = c("High", "High", "High", "High", "High",
         "Low", "Low", "Low", "Low", "Low"))
plotHistogramCustom(d2, variable = "MW", group_by = "GI")

# 4 groups: Kruskal-Wallis + post-hoc
d3 <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 320, 350, 600, 620, 650, 400, 420, 450, 480, 500, 520),
  Class = rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 3))
plotHistogramCustom(d3, variable = "MW", group_by = "Class")

# Suppress console
plotHistogramCustom(d2, variable = "MW", group_by = "GI",
                    console_stats = FALSE)



plotViolin()
Violin plot with automatic Wilcoxon / Kruskal-Wallis selection.

# 2 groups: Wilcoxon
d2 <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 320, 350, 380, 400, 500, 520, 550, 580, 600),
  GI = c("High", "High", "High", "High", "High",
         "Low", "Low", "Low", "Low", "Low"))
plotViolin(d2, variable = "MW", group_by = "GI")

# 4 groups: Kruskal-Wallis + post-hoc
d4 <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 320, 350, 600, 620, 650, 400, 420, 450, 480, 500, 520),
  Class = rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 3))
plotViolin(d4, variable = "MW", group_by = "Class",
           show_box = TRUE, show_points = TRUE)



plotPCA()
PCA chemical space plot with PERMANOVA and loading arrows.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 400, 500, 350, 450, 380, 320, 420, 480, 360),
  LogP = c(2, 3, 4, 2.5, 3.5, 2.8, 2.2, 3.2, 3.8, 2.6),
  TPSA = c(60, 80, 100, 70, 90, 65, 55, 75, 95, 68),
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 5))

plotPCA(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"), color_by = "group")
plotPCA(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"),
        color_by = "group", scale_data = FALSE)
plotPCA(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"),
        color_by = "group", console_stats = FALSE)



plotTSNE()
t-SNE chemical space with PERMANOVA.

set.seed(42)
d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(rnorm(25, 350, 50), rnorm(25, 500, 50)),
  LogP = c(rnorm(25, 2.5, 1), rnorm(25, 4.5, 1)),
  TPSA = c(rnorm(25, 70, 20), rnorm(25, 100, 20)),
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 25))

plotTSNE(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"),
         color_by = "group", perplexity = 5)



plotUMAP()
UMAP chemical space with PERMANOVA.

set.seed(42)
d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(rnorm(25, 350, 50), rnorm(25, 500, 50)),
  LogP = c(rnorm(25, 2.5, 1), rnorm(25, 4.5, 1)),
  TPSA = c(rnorm(25, 70, 20), rnorm(25, 100, 20)),
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 25))

plotUMAP(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"),
         color_by = "group", n_neighbors = 10)



plotParallel()
Parallel coordinates plot with PERMANOVA.

d <- data.frame(
  MW = c(300, 400, 500, 350, 450, 380),
  LogP = c(2, 3, 4, 2.5, 3.5, 2.8),
  TPSA = c(60, 80, 100, 70, 90, 65),
  group = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"))

plotParallel(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"), color_by = "group")
plotParallel(d, variables = c("MW", "LogP", "TPSA"),
             color_by = "group", scale_data = FALSE)



plotRadar()
Radar chart comparing up to 5 molecules.

d <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Aspirin", "Ibuprofen", "Caffeine"),
  MW = c(180, 206, 194),
  LogP = c(1.2, 3.5, 0.1),
  TPSA = c(63, 37, 62),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 1, 6),
  `#H-bond donors` = c(1, 0, 0),
  `#Rotatable bonds` = c(3, 4, 0),
  check.names = FALSE)

plotRadar(d, id_col = "Name",
          ids = c("Aspirin", "Ibuprofen", "Caffeine"))



plotTanimoto()
Tanimoto similarity / AGNES clustering dendrogram.

d <- data.frame(
  Name = c("ethanol", "aspirin", "benzene", "toluene", "phenol"),
  SMILES = c("CCO", "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "c1ccccc1",
            "Cc1ccccc1", "Oc1ccccc1"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Different linkage methods
plotTanimoto(d, smiles_col = "SMILES", label_col = "Name",
             method = "average")
plotTanimoto(d, smiles_col = "SMILES", label_col = "Name",
             method = "complete")
plotTanimoto(d, smiles_col = "SMILES", label_col = "Name",
             method = "single")
plotTanimoto(d, smiles_col = "SMILES", label_col = "Name",
             method = "ward")



plotClusterHeatmap()
Cluster heatmap with dendrogram using pheatmap.

d <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Drug A", "Drug B", "Drug C", "Drug D", "Drug E",
           "Drug F", "Drug G", "Drug H"),
  MW = c(300, 350, 600, 320, 450, 380, 500, 410),
  LogP = c(2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 2.5, 4.5, 3.5),
  TPSA = c(50, 60, 120, 40, 90, 70, 100, 80),
  MR = c(70, 85, 130, 65, 100, 80, 110, 95),
  check.names = FALSE)

# Basic
plotClusterHeatmap(d, id_col = "Name")

# With cell values and cutting
plotClusterHeatmap(d, id_col = "Name", display_numbers = TRUE,
                   cutree_rows = 2, palette = "viridis")

# With correlation distance
plotClusterHeatmap(d, id_col = "Name",
                   clustering_distance = "correlation",
                   method = "average")

# With annotation
d$Class <- c("A", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "B")
plotClusterHeatmap(d, id_col = "Name",
                   annotation_row = "Class", cutree_rows = 2)

title: Learning Guide
text:
ADMET Properties

computeADMETProperties()
Computes BOILED-Egg ADMET classification (GI absorption, BBB permeant, Pgp substrate).

d <- data.frame(LogP = c(2, 5), TPSA = c(50, 150), MW = c(300, 500),
                `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 5),
                `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 10),
                check.names = FALSE)
d <- computeADMETProperties(d)

title: Learning Guide
text:
Report Generation

generateReport()
Generates a comprehensive report (HTML, PDF, or Word) from one or more datasets.

d <- data.frame(
  Name = c("druglike", "violator"),
  SMILES = c("CCO", "CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC"),
  MW = c(300, 650), LogP = c(2, 7), TPSA = c(40, 160),
  MR = c(70, 150),
  `#H-bond acceptors` = c(4, 12), `#H-bond donors` = c(2, 7),
  `#Rotatable bonds` = c(3, 14), `#Heavy atoms` = c(20, 80),
  `#Aromatic heavy atoms` = c(6, 9),
  check.names = FALSE)
d <- computeViolationColumns(d)

# HTML report
generateReport(d, filters = c("Lipinski", "Veber"),
               format = "html", source_name = "Example")

title: admetshiny
text:
admetshiny is an open-source R package designed to accelerate drug discovery workflows by unifying programmatic tools and an intuitive dual-interface Shiny application.












Note🔬 Descriptor Calculation



Integrates seamlessly with CDK and Webchem to compute comprehensive molecular descriptors directly within R.










Note🛠 Data Standardization



Standardizes heterogeneous ADMET datasets using the integrated ADMET Master Manager.










Note💊 Drug-Likeness Filtering



Applies established filters, including Lipinski’s and Veber’s rules, for rapid candidate triaging.










Note🧪 PK Endpoint Prediction



Predicts key pharmacokinetic parameters, such as P-glycoprotein substrates and BOILED-Egg models.








Automate statistical workflows and generate publication-ready figures with a single command or click:

Dimensionality Reduction: Automated PCA and UMAP projections.
Hierarchical Clustering: AGNES dendrograms based on Tanimoto similarity matrices.
Automated Reporting: Export comprehensive statistical reports instantly.

title: 🌿 The Flagship Species
text:
🌱 Species Overview
The frailejón is a caulescent rosette reaching up to 4 m in height, with slender stems, inflorescences approximately equal in length to the leaves, and yellow capitula.






NoteEcological significance



It is one of the emblematic plants of the Colombian páramo ecosystem, playing a key role in water regulation, storage, and generation.





Espeletia hartwegiana in its natural páramo habitat

title: 🌿 The Flagship Species
text:
🦋 A Keystone of High-Andean Biodiversity
Beyond its ecological function, E. hartwegiana supports a unique assemblage of microorganisms, insects, birds, and other high-Andean organisms that depend on páramo habitats.
The species is also an important reservoir of specialized secondary metabolites with promising pharmacological and biotechnological potential.

title: 🌿 The Flagship Species
text:
⚠️ Conservation Threats
Natural populations throughout the northern Andes are under increasing pressure from:

🌡️ Climate change
🚜 Agricultural expansion
🐄 Livestock grazing
🔥 Recurrent fires
🧩 Habitat fragmentation







WarningUpward habitat shift



Rising temperatures are expected to reduce suitable páramo habitats, forcing populations to migrate to higher elevations where available habitat becomes increasingly limited.





Threats to páramo ecosystems

section: ⚙️ Principal Functions of ADMETShiny in R
text:
⚙️ Principal Functions of ADMETShiny in R
With ADMETShiny, say goodbye to manual ADMET analysis spread across multiple web servers. Manage all your physicochemical profiles in a single place.





Once your analysis is complete, you can generate a single consolidated report summarizing the main characteristics of each model.






Tip🔒 No external websites needed



Don’t want to submit your compounds to external websites? Don’t worry. ADMETShiny includes a local web server built with the rCDK R package and the Java SE Development Kit (JDK), so your profiles can be estimated entirely on your own machine.

Input method

🔬 Molecular retrieval

title: Changelog
text:
v1.1.0 (Beta - Accessible via the remotes package)

Cluster Heatmap (plotClusterHeatmap)

Replaced base R heatmap() with pheatmap::pheatmap() for publication-quality rendering.
12 new parameters: display_numbers, number_format, cutree_rows, cutree_cols, clustering_distance, border_color, na_col, show_rownames, show_colnames, angle_col, fontsize, annotation_row.
Cophenetic correlation coefficient (Sokal & Rohlf, 1962) reported in the heatmap title for both rows and columns.
Distance metric selector: euclidean, correlation (1 - Pearson), manhattan, maximum, canberra, binary, minkowski.
Row annotation support: pass a column name or data.frame to colour-code compound groups.
Cell values can be displayed inside each cell with configurable format.
Dendrogram cutting: cutree_rows and cutree_cols draw coloured borders.
Added "Dark2" and "Spectral" palettes.
Duplicate compound names detected and reported via message().
Shiny UI expanded with dedicated controls in both modules.



Histogram Statistics (plotHistogramCustom)

Automatic test selection: 2 groups -> Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U); >= 3 groups -> Kruskal-Wallis; ungrouped -> Shapiro-Wilk.
n_groups and Mean +/- SD shown in the subtitle.
safe_shapiro() helper handles edge cases (n < 3, n > 5000, constant data).



Violin Plot Statistics (plotViolin)

Same Wilcoxon / Kruskal-Wallis / Shapiro-Wilk logic as the histogram.
Numeric coercion of the variable column.
Filtered data used for plotting.



Correlation Heatmap (plotCorrHeatmap)

New method parameter: "pearson" (default) or "spearman".
Significance testing via cor.test() for each pair of descriptors.
Significance asterisks in each cell.
Method name shown in the title; significance legend in the subtitle.
Shiny UI: correlation method selector in both modules.



BOILED-Egg (plotBoiledEgg)

Y-axis label dynamically switches to "WLOGP" when WLOGP polygons are selected.



PERMANOVA in PCA, t-SNE, UMAP and Parallel Coordinates

PERMANOVA (Anderson 2001) computed via vegan::adonis2() on the scaled descriptor distance matrix.
Results (R-squared, F, p-value) shown in the plot subtitle.
Post-hoc pairwise PERMANOVA with Holm correction when the main test is significant and >= 3 groups.



Drug-likeness Filters: Violation Column Preservation

computeViolationColumns() preserves pre-existing violation columns from data sources.
Column mapping UI includes options for Lipinski, Ghose, Veber, Egan and Muegge Violations.



Console Output (R console)

Statistical results printed to the R console with cli formatting.
Detailed output for: histogram, violin, correlation heatmap, BOILED-Egg, PCA, t-SNE, UMAP and parallel coordinates.
Each report includes: descriptive statistics, normality assessment, significance test with effect size, post-hoc comparisons, interpretation and bibliographic reference.



Report Generation

New “Statistical Analysis” section in the generated report.
Includes group comparisons, post-hoc, correlation summary and PERMANOVA results.
Six new bibliographic references.



Package Documentation

Hexagonal logo added to the package-level help page (?admetshiny).




Removed packages

Removed the base R heatmap(); pheatmap is now required.




v1.0.1

Added PERMANOVA statistics (R2, F, p-value) to PCA, t-SNE and UMAP plots via vegan::adonis2(), computed on the original distance matrix.
Added cumUlative R2 to the PCA subtitle.
Added Shapiro-Wilk normality test and descriptive statistics (n, mean, SD, median, IQR) to plotMW, plotTPSA and plotLogP subtitles.
Added Kruskal-Wallis test to plotHistogramCustom and plotViolinsubtitles, Wilcoxon, test for the two-group colour support.
Improved the cluster heatmap with a labelled colour key (key.title, key.xlab), finer colour breaks, and NA colour support.
Fixed plotClusterHeatmap to handle NULL inputs from renderUI (method, palette, scale_data) with safe defaults.
Increased report figure resolution from 150 to 300 dpi.


Dark mode

Fixed the report preview container showing invisible text in dark mode (white background with light text).




PubChem / WebChem compatibility update

Updated pc_prop() property names for webchem 2.0: CanonicalSMILES is now ConnectivitySMILES. IsomericSMILES is now SMILES. Added column rename for backwards compatibility.



New dependencies

Added vegan to Imports for PERMANOVA computation.
Added importFrom for stats::as.hclust, stats::cophenetic, stats::rect.hclust, stats::kruskal.test, stats::quantile, stats::shapiro.test, stats::wilcox.test.
Added importFrom for vegan::adonis2()




v1.0.0

Initial CRAN release.
Interactive Shiny application with two complementary modules: CDK & webchem and ADMET Master Manager.
Drug-likeness filters: Lipinski, Veber, Ghose, Egan, Muegge.
BOILED-Egg model with dual WLOGP / ALogP polygon systems.
P-glycoprotein substrate prediction via an embedded Random Forest classifier.
PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, parallel coordinates, violin, radar, custom histogram, cluster heatmap and correlation heatmap visualizations.
Tanimoto / AGNES structural-similarity clustering.
Comprehensive HTML / PDF / Word report generation.
Dark mode, custom colour palettes and high-resolution figure export.
Codename: Espeletia hartwegiana.

title: Theoretical Foundations
text: This document describes the scientific basis and algorithms underlying the admetshiny package.

title: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Drug-Likeness Filters

Lipinski Rule of Five (1997)
Reference: Lipinski, C. A., Lombardo, F., Dominy, B. W., & Feeney, P. J. (1997). Experimental and computational approaches to estimate solubility and permeability in drug discovery and development settings. Advanced Drug Delivery Reviews, 23(1-3), 3-25.
Criteria:



Parameter
Threshold




Molecular Weight (MW)
<= 500 Da


LogP
<= 5


H-bond Acceptors (HBA)
<= 10


H-bond Donors (HBD)
<= 5



Implementation: A compound violates if any criterion exceeds the threshold. Up to 1 violation is generally considered acceptable.


Ghose Filter (1999)
Reference: Ghose, A. K., Viswanadhan, V. N., & Wendoloski, J. J. (1999). A knowledge-based approach in designing combinatorial or medicinal chemistry libraries for drug discovery. Journal of Combinatorial Chemistry, 1(1), 55-68.
Criteria:



Parameter
Range




Molecular Weight
160 - 480 Da


Molar Refractivity (MR)
40 - 130


LogP
-0.4 to 5.6


Total Atoms
20 - 70



Note: The atom count refers to TOTAL atoms (heavy + hydrogens), consistent with the MW range. The filter prefers "#Total atoms" when available and falls back to "#Heavy atoms".


Veber Filter (2002)
Reference: Veber, D. F., Johnson, S. R., Cheng, H. Y., Smith, B. R., Ward, K. W., & Kopple, K. D. (2002). Molecular properties that influence the oral bioavailability of drug candidates. Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, 45(12), 2615-2623.
Criteria:



Parameter
Threshold




Rotatable Bonds (RB)
<= 10


TPSA OR HBA + HBD
<= 140 OR <= 12



Note: The two polarity conditions are alternatives (OR), not cumulative, following the original paper.


Egan Filter (2000)
Reference: Egan, W. J., Merz, K. M., & Baldwin, J. J. (2000). Prediction of drug absorption using multivariate statistics. Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, 43(21), 3867-3877.
Criteria:



Parameter
Threshold




TPSA
<= 131.6


LogP
<= 5.88





Muegge Filter (2001)
Reference: Muegge, I., Heald, S. L., & Brittelli, D. (2001). Simple selection criteria for drug-like chemical matter. Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, 44(12), 1841-1846.
Criteria:



Parameter
Range/Threshold




MW
200 - 600


LogP
-2 to 5


HBA
<= 10


HBD
<= 5


Rotatable Bonds
<= 15


TPSA
<= 150


Pharmacophore points
>= 4



Note: Pharmacophore points are approximated as HBA + HBD (rings and hydrophobic centers are not directly available from CDK descriptors).

title: Theoretical Foundations
text:
BOILED-Egg Model

Original Publication
Reference: Daina, A., & Zoete, V. (2016). A boiled egg to predict gastrointestinal absorption and brain penetration of small molecules. ChemMedChem, 11(11), 1117-1121.


WLOGP Polygons (Official)
The original BOILED-Egg was calibrated with WLOGP (Wildman-Crippen LogP). The official polygon coordinates are from the supplementary data (Data S3) of Daina & Zoete (2016). These define two elliptical regions in the TPSA-LogP space:

White region (yolk): Compounds predicted to be absorbed by the GI tract (HIA+)
Yellow region (white): Compounds predicted to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB+)



ALogP Polygons (Trained)
When WLOGP is not available (e.g., CDK descriptors use ALogP), the package uses ALogP-trained polygons. These were trained using Monte Carlo optimization on experimental HIA and BBB data.
Training data: 659 HIA compounds and 256 BBB compounds from Daina & Zoete (2016).
Optimization method: Monte Carlo + Metropolis algorithm.


P-glycoprotein Substrate Prediction
Reference: Seelig, A. (1998). A general pattern for substrate recognition by P-glycoprotein. European Journal of Biochemistry, 251(1-2), 252-261.
The package uses an embedded Random Forest classifier trained from experimental data.

title: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Statistical Methods

PERMANOVA (Anderson 2001)
Reference: Anderson, M. J. (2001). A new method for non-parametric multivariate analysis of variance. Austral Ecology, 26, 32-46.
Implementation: vegan::adonis2() on Euclidean distance of z-scored descriptors. 999 permutations.


Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Mann-Whitney U)
Reference: Mann, H. B., & Whitney, D. R. (1947). On a test of whether one of two random variables is stochastically larger than the other. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 18(1), 50-60.
Use: Comparing 2 groups (non-parametric alternative to t-test).


Kruskal-Wallis Test
Reference: Kruskal, W. H., & Wallis, W. A. (1952). Use of ranks in one-criterion variance analysis. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 47(260), 583-621.
Use: Comparing >= 3 groups (non-parametric alternative to ANOVA).
Effect size: eta-squared = H / (N - 1).


Post-hoc: Pairwise Wilcoxon with Holm Correction
Use: After significant Kruskal-Wallis (p < 0.05), identifies which specific pairs differ.
Correction: Holm-Bonferroni method for multiple comparisons.


Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test
Reference: Shapiro, S. S., & Wilk, M. B. (1965). An analysis of variance test for normality. Biometrika, 52(3-4), 591-611.
Use: Tests whether a variable follows a normal distribution.


Cophenetic Correlation
Reference: Sokal, R. R., & Rohlf, F. J. (1962). The comparison of dendrograms by objective methods. Taxon, 11(2), 33-40.
Use: Measures how faithfully a dendrogram preserves the original pairwise distances. Values close to 1.0 indicate a good fit.


Pearson Correlation
Reference: Pearson, K. (1895). Notes on regression and inheritance in the case of two parents. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 58, 240-242.


Spearman Rank Correlation
Reference: Spearman, C. (1904). The proof and measurement of association between two things. American Journal of Psychology, 15(1), 72-101.

title: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Tanimoto Similarity
Reference: Willett, P., Barnard, J. M., & Downs, G. M. (1998). Chemical similarity searching. Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences, 38(6), 983-996.
Implementation: Extended fingerprints computed via rcdk, Tanimoto similarity matrix, AGNES hierarchical clustering.

AGNES Linking Methods







Method
Description




average (UPGMA)
Average distance between clusters; balanced


complete
Maximum distance (furthest neighbour); tight clusters


single
Minimum distance (nearest neighbour); chaining effect


ward
Minimizes within-cluster variance; compact spherical clusters

title: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Additional Metrics

Pfizer 3/75 Rule
Reference: Hughes, J. D., et al. (2008). Estimating the toxicity of compounds. Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry Letters, 18(17), 4872-4875.
Criteria: LogP < 3 AND TPSA > 75.


GSK 4/400 Rule
Reference: Gleeson, M. P., et al. (2011). Drug-likeness. Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, 54(13), 4459-4468.
Criteria: MW <= 400 AND LogP <= 4.


Golden Triangle
Reference: Johnson, T. W., et al. (2009). Using the Golden Triangle. Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry Letters, 19(17), 4872-4875.
Criteria: MW 200-450 AND LogP -2 to 4.5 (oral bioavailability zone).


Lead-Likeness
Reference: Teague, S. J., et al. (1999). The design of leadlike combinatorial libraries. Angewandte Chemie International Edition, 38(24), 3743-3748.
Criteria: MW <= 450 AND LogP <= 4.5 AND rotatable bonds <= 10.
